In supervised learning, the two main tasks differ in the type of output they produce:

* **Classification** – the model assigns each input to one of a *finite set of discrete classes* (e.g., “spam” vs. “not‑spam”, “sick” vs. “healthy”). The learning algorithm is trained on labeled examples and outputs either a class label or a probability for each class.  
  [Passage 1]

* **Regression** – the model predicts a *real‑valued target* (e.g., house price, temperature). The learning algorithm is trained on labeled examples and outputs a continuous numeric value.

1.3 How Supervised Learning Works
In this section, I brieﬂy explain how supervised learning works so that you have the picture
of the whole process before we go into detail. I decided to use supervised learning as an
example because it’s the type of machine learning most frequently used in practice.
The supervised learning process starts with gathering the data. The data for supervised
learning is a collection of pairs (input, output). Input could be anything, for example, email
messages, pictures, or sensor measurements. Outputs are usually real numbers, or labels (e.g.
“spam”, “not_spam”, “cat”, “dog”, “mouse”, etc). In some cases, outputs are vectors (e.g.,
four coordinates of the rectangle around a person on the picture), sequences (e.g. [“adjective”,
“adjective”, “noun”] for the input “big beautiful car”), or have some other structure.

Parameters are the internal variables of a model that are **learned directly from the training data** by the learning algorithm. They define the model itself and are updated during training [Passage 1].

Hyperparameters, on the other hand, are **settings that are not learned from the data** but are chosen (or tuned) separately—typically by evaluating performance on validation data. For example, the scalar γ in a combined cost function is treated as a hyperparameter and its value is tuned on validation data rather than being learned directly by the algorithm [Passage 3].

2.9 Shallow vs. Deep Learning
A shallow learning algorithm learns the parameters of the model directly from the features
of the training examples. Most supervised learning algorithms are shallow. The notorious
exceptions are neural network learning algorithms, speciﬁcally those that build neural
networks with more than one layer between input and output. Such neural networks are
called deep neural networks. In deep neural network learning (or, simply, deep learning),
contrary to shallow learning, most model parameters are learned not directly from the features
of the training examples, but from the outputs of the preceding layers.
Don’t worry if you don’t understand what that means right now. We look at neural networks
more closely in Chapter 6.

8.7 Transfer Learning
Transfer learning is probably where neural networks have a unique advantage over the
shallow models. In transfer learning, you pick an existing model trained on some dataset,
and you adapt this model to predict examples from another dataset, diﬀerent from the one
the model was built on. This second dataset is not like holdout sets you use for validation
and test. It may represent some other phenomenon, or, as machine learning scientists say, it
may come from another statistical distribution.
For example, imagine you have trained your model to recognize (and label) wild animals on a
big labeled dataset. After some time, you have another problem to solve: you need to build a
model that would recognize domestic animals. With shallow learning algorithms, you do not

separate well new positive and negative examples from one another. For other, less likely
situations, our model will make errors, but because such situations are less likely, the number
of errors will likely be smaller than the number of correct predictions.
Intuitively, the larger is the set of training examples, the more unlikely that the new examples
will be dissimilar to (and lie on the plot far from) the examples used for training.

Cross-validation works like follows. First, you ﬁx the values of the hyperparameters you want
to evaluate. Then you split your training set into several subsets of the same size. Each
subset is called a fold. Typically, ﬁve-fold cross-validation is used in practice. With ﬁve-fold
cross-validation, you randomly split your training data into ﬁve folds: {F1,F2,...,F5}. Each
Fk, k = 1,..., 5 contains 20% of your training data. Then you train ﬁve models as follows.
To train the ﬁrst model, f1, you use all examples from folds F2, F3, F4, and F5 as the training
set and the examples from F1 as the validation set. To train the second model, f2, you
use the examples from folds F1, F3, F4, and F5 to train and the examples from F2 as the
validation set. You continue building models iteratively like this and compute the value of
the metric of interest on each validation set, from F1 to F5. Then you average the ﬁve values
of the metric to get the ﬁnal value.

8.7 Transfer Learning
Transfer learning is probably where neural networks have a unique advantage over the
shallow models. In transfer learning, you pick an existing model trained on some dataset,
and you adapt this model to predict examples from another dataset, diﬀerent from the one
the model was built on. This second dataset is not like holdout sets you use for validation
and test. It may represent some other phenomenon, or, as machine learning scientists say, it
may come from another statistical distribution.
For example, imagine you have trained your model to recognize (and label) wild animals on a
big labeled dataset. After some time, you have another problem to solve: you need to build a
model that would recognize domestic animals. With shallow learning algorithms, you do not

separate well new positive and negative examples from one another. For other, less likely
situations, our model will make errors, but because such situations are less likely, the number
of errors will likely be smaller than the number of correct predictions.
Intuitively, the larger is the set of training examples, the more unlikely that the new examples
will be dissimilar to (and lie on the plot far from) the examples used for training.

Classification and regression in supervised learning are distinguished by the nature of the output they produce. Classification involves predicting a label from a set of predefined classes, while regression predicts a continuous value. This is explained in [Passage 1] and [Passage 2]. 

[Passage 1] states that classification is about "automatically assigning a label to an unlabeled example," and regression is about "predicting a real-valued label (often called a target) given an unlabeled example." 

[Passage 2] further elaborates, stating that classification involves "automatically assigning a label to an unlabeled example," and regression is about "estimating house price valuation based on house features." 

Therefore, classification is about predicting a category or class label, whereas regression is about predicting a continuous value.

In this section, I brieﬂy explain how supervised learning works so that you have the picture
of the whole process before we go into detail. I decided to use supervised learning as an
example because it’s the type of machine learning most frequently used in practice.
The supervised learning process starts with gathering the data. The data for supervised

2.8 Model-Based vs. Instance-Based Learning
Most supervised learning algorithms are model-based. We have already seen one such
algorithm: SVM. Model-based learning algorithms use the training data to create a model
that has parameters learned from the training data. In SVM, the two parameters we saw
were w∗ and b∗. After the model was built, the training data can be discarded.
Instance-based learning algorithms use the whole dataset as the model. One instance-based
algorithm frequently used in practice is k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN). In classiﬁcation, to
predict a label for an input example the kNN algorithm looks at the close neighborhood of
the input example in the space of feature vectors and outputs the label that it saw the most
often in this close neighborhood.

The kernel trick is a technique that lets an SVM handle data that is not linearly separable in its original space by implicitly mapping the data into a higher‑dimensional space during the optimization process. Instead of explicitly transforming each input vector into that high‑dimensional space, a kernel function computes the inner product of the transformed vectors directly. This allows the SVM algorithm to find a linear decision boundary in the transformed space, which corresponds to a non‑linear boundary in the original space, without incurring the computational cost of the explicit transformation.
